title: Research Bite #7: Attention Contagion
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #7 covers Kasli, Forrin, and colleagues' study “Attention Contagion Online: Attention Spreads Between Students in a Virtual Classroom,” which finds that a student's attentiveness in a virtual lecture is socially contagious even through small webcam thumbnails. Students who watched a lecture alongside visibly attentive classmates (confederates planted by the researchers) reported being more attentive themselves, spent less time media-multitasking, and scored meaningfully higher on a subsequent content quiz — over one full letter grade higher (79% vs. 67%) — than students who watched alongside visibly inattentive classmates. The authors attribute the effect to two social mechanisms: goal contagion, where observing a classmate's on-task behavior activates the same goal in the observer, and conformity, where students adjust their own behavior to match a perceived social norm. Because the effect operates through visible cues, it has direct design implications for online teaching — visible, attentive teaching assistants, encouraging webcams to stay on, and even hiding the video of visibly inattentive students are all levers a virtual classroom can pull. Barton's takeaway is that attention in a virtual classroom is not a private, individual state — it is a social signal that spreads, for better or worse, exactly the way it does in a physical room.
points: Students who watched a lecture alongside attentive classmates scored over one letter grade higher on a subsequent quiz (79% vs. 67%) than those alongside inattentive classmates — a substantial, directly measurable learning consequence of a purely social cue.
The effect operates even through small webcam thumbnails, meaning students are picking up and responding to remarkably subtle visual signals of a classmate's engagement.

Two named mechanisms drive the contagion — goal contagion (observing a peer's on-task behavior activates the same goal) and conformity (adjusting behavior to match a perceived social norm) — giving teachers a vocabulary for why visible engagement matters, not just that it does.

The practical design implications are concrete: keep teaching assistants visibly attentive on camera, encourage students to enable webcams, and consider software features that hide the video feed of visibly inattentive students to stop the contagion from spreading the other way.

Simply informing students that attention is contagious is itself proposed as an intervention — awareness of the effect may motivate students to limit inattentive behavior out of consideration for classmates, not just themselves.

The study found that students who see other classmates behaving attentively during an online lecture are more likely to report being attentive themselves, spend less time multitasking, and score higher on a subsequent quiz.
Students are very aware of their classmates’ attentiveness, even through small webcam thumbnails. Attention is highly contagious in virtual classrooms.
The effects of this attention contagion are significant, with students in the study who saw attentive classmates performing much better on a quiz than those who saw inattentive classmates.

Students who watched the lecture with attentive (vs. inattentive) confederates were more attentive, spent less time media multitasking (i.e., checking other websites and their phone), and, importantly, performed meaningfully better on a lecture-content quiz (by over one letter grade: 79% vs. 67%).
Instructors can reduce inattentiveness by hiding the webcam videos of inattentive students. This could be a feature of videoconferencing software.
Teachers should inform students about attention contagion. This may motivate students to limit their inattentive behaviors to avoid negatively affecting their classmates.
